SM19L-A1.free_elimination: -6 and 38 struck by a pattern tell: the parameter appears only as (k - 2), so candidate answers come as 2 +/- t, and -4 / 8 are the only pair in the set symmetric about 2. Plug-back confirms cheaply ((k-2)^2 is 64 for -6 and 1296 for 38, never 36). What survives is exactly the item's decision: 8 (coincident lines) vs -4 (parallel distinct), which needs the constant-ratio check (15/5 = 3 = (k-2)/2 at k = 8).
SM19L-A1.note: Cold solve: proportional coefficients need (k-2)/2 = 18/(k-2), (k-2)^2 = 36, k = 8 or -4. k = 8: 6x+18y=15 is 3*(2x+6y=5), same line, infinitely many. k = -4: -6x+18y=15 vs 2x-6y=5, ratio -3 on coefficients but -3*5 = -15 != 15, parallel distinct, no solution. Key -4 correct and unique (every other k gives a unique solution). Decision point is real: the student who takes the positive root lands on 8. Distractor paths all reach their values. BLUEPRINT (asked): the quadratic is (k-2)^2 = 36, a pure square solved by a square root, no factoring; the tested skill is the solution count of a system of two linear equations, which is squarely Algebra. On blueprint, borderline only in that the parameter appears squared; I would keep it. REPAIR for the pair tell: add a second pair symmetric about 2 from a real error so the symmetry no longer singles out the key's pair. Cross-multiplying as division, (k-2)^2 = 18/2 = 9, gives k-2 = +/-3, k = 5 or -1. Set {-4, -1, 5, 8}: two pairs each symmetric about 2; no member is the mean, sum, difference or double of others (means of pairs are 2, not in set; differences 3, 6, 9, 12, not in set); parity splits evenly; two negatives. Which pair is right needs the proportion; which member needs the constant check. Distractor_solve for -1/5: 2 - Math.sqrt(18/2), 2 + Math.sqrt(18/2).

SM19L-A2.free_elimination: none. Two integers and two thirds; no member is a mean, sum, difference or double of others (28/3 - 13/3 = 5, 20 - 8 = 12, neither in the set); no sign or magnitude bound in the stem; 20 = 12/3 + 16 needs b = 16 first, so it is not a free strike.
SM19L-A2.note: Cold solve: LHS 3ax - 6 + b, RHS (12 - 2b)x + 10. Constants: b = 16. x-coefficients: 3a = 12 - 32 = -20, a = -20/3. a + b = 28/3. All three distractor paths reproduce (20: drops -2bx; 8: 3 distributed only to ax, b = 12, a = -4; 13/3: -2(bx - 5) expanded as -2bx - 5, b = 1, a = 10/3). Option set is clean. DIFFICULTY: there is no decision point. The routine procedure (expand both sides fully, match x-coefficients and constants) reaches the key directly; the explanation's 'use the constant terms first' is the order any student solving a 2x2 by substitution picks anyway. Every distractor is a distribution slip, which tests care, not judgment. Medium. REPAIR: relabel medium (it is a sound medium item). To make it hard, the condition must create a fork the routine misses, e.g. ask for no solution with one constant fixed so that the student must require the x-coefficients to match and the constants to DIFFER, and include the infinitely-many value as a distractor - but that is a different item and would need its own audit.

SM19L-A3.free_elimination: 17 (soft). Monotonicity: f(x-3) - f(x+2) = 20 > 0 shows at a glance that the smaller input gives the larger output, so f is decreasing. 17 > 9, so it needs the known point to sit right of x = 6, and the only reading that does that (point at input 10) gives 9 + 16 = 25 under a decreasing f, not 17. Put plainly, 17 exists only on the wrong-slope-sign path, and the slope sign is readable without arithmetic. -7 also needs m = +4 but is < 9, so it does not die the same way. No closure: the set is symmetric about -3 (means of -23/17 and -7/1 are both -3) but -3 is not an option.
SM19L-A3.note: Cold solve: f = mx + c, f(x-3) - f(x+2) = -5m = 20, m = -4. (4, 9) on y = f(x-6) means f(-2) = 9. f(6) = 9 + 8(-4) = -23. Correct and unique. Distractor paths reproduce (1: f(4) = 9; 17: m = +4 with f(4) = 9; -7: m = +4 with f(10) = 9). Hard: reading the shift (input 4 on f(x-6) is input -2 on f) is a real decision, and the obvious mistake f(4) = 9 lands on 1. Desmos does not bypass it. Blueprint: linear functions, on. REPAIR for 17: replace it with a value below 9 that a decreasing-f error reaches. The obvious swap does NOT work: with the slope right, the three shift readings put the point at inputs -2, 4, 10, which gives -23, 1, 25, an arithmetic progression. Then 1 is the mean of the other two, so the main distractor dies by closure. Workable swap: 7, from reading y = f(x-6) as y = f(x) - 6, so f(4) = 15 and f(6) = 15 - 8 = 7. This survives monotonicity (7 < 9). Set {-23, -7, 1, 7}: no member is a mean, sum, difference or double of others. Caveat: it creates an x/-x pair (-7, 7), which points a guesser AWAY from the key, so it strikes nothing, but the gate should see it. distractor_solve: 'const m = 20/((-3) - 2); return (9 + 6) + m*(6 - 4);'.

SM19L-A4.free_elimination: -25 and -5 together, by monotonicity. h falls (11 then 3) and g falls (slope -2), so f must rise; that is a sign rule, not arithmetic. g(1) = 2 is one step, so f(2) = 11, and an increasing f gives f(10) > 11. Both negatives die. They are exactly the two distractors built on a negative slope for f, so one sign decision removes two of the three distractors. 17 vs 27 survives and needs the anchor (f(-2) = 3, not f(3) = 3).
SM19L-A4.note: Cold solve: g(1) = 2 and g(3) = -2, so f(2) = 11 and f(-2) = 3. Slope of f = 8/4 = 2, f(x) = 2x + 7, f(10) = 27. Correct and unique. Distractor paths reproduce (-25: h values read as f values, slope -4; -5: p = -2; 17: p = 2 but anchored at f(3) = 3). DIFFICULTY: the routine procedure (compute g(1) and g(3), which gives two points of f, then the line through them) needs no decision at all. The only trap catches a student who treats h as f, which a competent student does not do. Medium. Blueprint: composition of linear functions stays linear, on. REPAIR: replace both negative-slope distractors with increasing-f errors above 11 so the sign decision strikes nothing. 29 = h(1) = 11 read as f(1) = 11 with the correct slope, so q = 9 (distractor_solve 'const p = 2; return p*10 + (11 - p*1);'). 19 = sign slip g(3) = +2, anchored at f(2) = 3, so q = -1 ('const p = 2; return p*10 + (3 - p*2);'). Set {17, 19, 27, 29}: all > 11 and all odd; pairwise means 18, 22, 23, 23, 24, 28 and differences 2, 8, 10, 12, none in the set. The set is symmetric about 23, which is not a member. Even repaired, it stays medium unless a decision point is added.

SM19L-A5.free_elimination: All three distractors, without the quadratic. (1) 8/3 is a one-step combination of the printed 8 and 3, and it zeroes the x-coefficient (0 >= 10, empty set). (2) 6: the set x <= k means dividing by (3k - 8) must flip the sign, so k < 8/3, and 6 dies. This is the item's intended decision, but it costs no arithmetic. (3) 15/7: the right side is visibly 15(k - 2). For 2 < k < 8/3 the boundary 15(k - 2)/(3k - 8) is positive over negative, so it is negative and cannot equal a positive k. 15/7 = 2.14 sits in that band and dies on sign alone. Only 5/3 survives, and the quadratic 3k^2 - 23k + 30 = 0 is never needed.
SM19L-A5.note: Cold solve: (3k - 8)x >= 15k - 30. Direction forces 3k - 8 < 0. Boundary (15k - 30)/(3k - 8) = k gives 3k^2 - 23k + 30 = 0 = (3k - 5)(k - 6), and only 5/3 is below 8/3. Check: -3x >= -5, so x <= 5/3. Correct and unique. Distractor paths reproduce, though '15/7 = 30/(15 - 1)' is a strained story. The direction fork is a genuine decision point, but the option set lets that fork plus a sign read finish the item, so the routine-procedure test never binds. Medium as it stands. BLUEPRINT (asked): off, being strict. Unlike A1 (a pure square solved by a square root), the intended route requires factoring or the quadratic formula on a non-monic 3k^2 - 23k + 30, which is Advanced Math (nonlinear equations in one variable). The linear inequality is only the wrapper. The 15/7 sign kill also means the intended route would not be how a strong student answers. REPAIR: keeping the two-root direction trap keeps the quadratic, so either move the item to Advanced Math or accept it is off-blueprint. Within the option set, any distractor with k <= 0 or 2 <= k < 8/3 dies by the sign argument, and any k > 8/3 dies by direction, so both non-6 distractors must lie in (0, 2) and come from named errors. One candidate: 30/23 (drops the 3k^2 term: 15k - 30 = -8k). It passes the sign test, and plugging it back gives boundary 120/47, which is not a glance. A second (0, 2) value from a real error was not found; sign-slip variants give irrational roots. Without one, n_struck stays at least 1 (8/3 or its replacement).

SM19L-A6.free_elimination: none from the option set. All four are halves; 51/2 and 53/2 are adjacent, but the stem promises no adjacency; no member is a mean, sum or double of others (51/2 - 37/2 = 7 is a printed constant, but a difference equal to a printed number strikes nothing). The real bypass is not an elimination, it is the whole item: see note.
SM19L-A6.note: Cold solve: 3*(eq1) - 5*(eq2) gives 2x - 14y = 21 + 30 = 51, so x - 7y = 51/2. Checked by solving at c = 0 (x = -11/10, y = -19/5, x - 7y = 25.5) and at c = 2 (x = 1.7, y = -3.4, 25.5). Correct, unique, independent of c. Distractor paths reproduce. DIFFICULTY: the stem says (x, y) is THE solution and asks for one number, so any test-taker can set c = 0 (or any value) and solve a plain 2x2, by hand or in Desmos, and land on the key. The c-cancelling combination is the elegant route but never the necessary one, and none of the distractors catches the substitute-a-value route. Medium at best, and arguably easy with Desmos. Blueprint: systems of two linear equations, on. REPAIR: no option swap fixes this; any 'combination independent of a free constant' item is bypassed by choosing the constant. Relabel medium, or retire from the hard pool.

SM19L-A7.free_elimination: 5 and 21/2, by glance plug-back. 5: k - 2 = 3 and 2k - 4 = 6 turn line 1 into line 2 (y = 3x + 6), which the stem's 'distinct' forbids. 21/2: 2k - 4 = 17 gives line 2 the same intercept as line 3, so those two meet at (0, 17), but line 1 always passes through (0, 6). Both are a single substitution plus reading an intercept. 23/2 survives (line 2 = 3x + 19 meets line 3 at x = -2/7, not a glance).
SM19L-A7.note: Cold solve: lines 1 and 2 give (k - 5)x = 2(k - 5), so for k != 5 they always cross at x = 2, at y = 2k + 2. Line 3 at x = 2 is 9, so k = 7/2. Check: (2, 9) is on y = 1.5x + 6, y = 3x + 3 and y = -4x + 17. Correct; k = 5 is excluded by 'distinct', so the answer is unique. Distractor paths reproduce. DIFFICULTY: the fixed point x = 2 is elegant but optional. The routine route (intersect lines 2 and 3, substitute into line 1) gives 2k^2 - 17k + 35 = 0 = (2k - 7)(k - 5), and the stem's explicit 'distinct' then discards 5, so a careful student reaches the key with no unflagged decision. A Desmos slider on k also finds it directly. Medium. BLUEPRINT (asked): on, borderline. The quadratic appears only on the 2-and-3 route; the most natural first step (intersect the two parameter lines) factors out (k - 5) and stays linear. That is weaker than A1's unavoidable square, and unlike A5 there is a linear route of equal length, so I keep it on the blueprint while noting that a student taking the 2-and-3 route must factor a non-monic quadratic. REPAIR: keep 5 (it is the quadratic-route trap; its glance kill is the stem working as written, though it still counts). Replace 21/2 with 35/2, from dividing (k - 5)x = 2(k - 5) to x = -2: line 3 gives y = 25, and line 2 at x = -2 gives 2k - 10 = 25 ('return (25 + 10)/2;'). Plug-back of 35/2 means solving a 2x2 (lines 2 and 3 meet at (-2, 25), line 1 gives -25), so it is not a glance. Set {7/2, 5, 23/2, 35/2}: pairwise means 17/4, 15/2, 21/2, 33/4, 45/4, 29/2, none in the set; differences 3/2, 13/2, 6, 8, 14, 25/2, none in the set. Even repaired, n_struck = 1 (5) and the item stays medium.

SM19L-A8.free_elimination: none. Two adjacent pairs (40/41, 43/44) but the stem promises no adjacency; no member is a mean, sum or double of others; the LP bound 44.08 needs the vertex solve and does not exclude 44 or 43 by itself; refuting 43 or 44 needs a lattice search, not a glance.
SM19L-A8.note: Cold solve: brute force over nonnegative integers. The maximum of 3x + 4y is 41, at (7, 5) only; 40 only at (8, 4); 42, 43 and 44 are unattainable. The vertex is (111/13, 60/13), profit 44.08. Correct and unique. Distractor paths reproduce (40 floor-rounds the vertex; 43 comes from (9, 4), which is infeasible at 71 > 69; 44 floors the vertex profit). Hard: the obvious procedure (find the corner, round down) lands on 40, and seeing that the integer optimum moves one step along the clay edge to (7, 5) is a real decision. Desmos shows the region but not the answer. BLUEPRINT: off, being strict. The constraints are Algebra content (linear inequalities in two variables), but maximizing a linear objective over the feasible region, and over the integer lattice at that, is linear programming. The Digital SAT asks which point satisfies a system, or the greatest value of one variable, not the optimum of a profit function. If an Algebra item is wanted, recast it to ask for the greatest y given x >= 7, or whether a stated plan is feasible; expect such a recast to drop to medium.
